stories.headline: ‘We spy on them too’: Trump shrugs off China-Iran satellite imagery report
stories.deck: President Trump has dismissed concerns regarding reports that Chinese entities are providing Iran with satellite imagery, suggesting that such espionage practices are not unlike those employed by the United States. This incident reportedly occurred just before a missile strike that resulted in the deaths of three American soldiers. With a meeting scheduled with Chinese President Xi Jinping, this…
stories.bodyText:
US President Donald Trump has downplayed a report that Chinese entities supplied Iran with satellite imagery of a US military base in Jordan before a July missile attack that killed three American soldiers, saying China’s spying on the US is no different from Washington’s intelligence activities.
“They basically do what we do,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One when asked about the report.
“You know what they say? That China spies on us,” Trump said. “I say you're right, and we spy on them, too.”
Trump was responding to a Wall Street Journal report citing US officials that Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery from Chinese entities before and after its July 17 missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in northeastern Jordan. Three US troops were killed and four wounded in the attack.
The report raises questions over whether Chinese satellite intelligence helped Iran target US military personnel. However, US officials cited by the Journal did not identify the Chinese entities involved or accuse Beijing of directly ordering or participating in the attack. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report.
Asked whether he would raise the issue with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump did not directly answer. 
Instead, he stressed the broader state of US-China ties and said Xi had “behaved reasonably well.”
“I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well,” Trump said.
The issue comes as Trump and Xi are expected to meet in the US on September 24. The meeting, which Beijing has yet to officially confirm, is expected to focus on stabilising ties between the world's two largest economies, with trade and technology among key issues.
The reported satellite link could add a sensitive security dimension to the talks, particularly because the alleged intelligence was connected to an attack that killed American service members.
For Trump, the timing also presents a diplomatic balancing act: Washington has concerns over Chinese entities allegedly assisting Iran with intelligence, while the US president appears keen to prevent the issue from escalating tensions with Xi before their meeting.
The key question now is whether the alleged transfer of satellite imagery represents routine Chinese intelligence activity or a more direct form of support to a US adversary, an issue that could test the fragile US-China relationship ahead of the summit.

stories.headline: Six years after 2020 heartbreak, Zverev beats Shelton to finally win US Open
stories.deck: Alexander Zverev triumphantly claimed his second Grand Slam title at the US Open, overcoming American contender Ben Shelton in a gritty four-set battle. This prestigious win not only solidified Zverev's comeback from his 2020 US Open final loss but also capped off an extraordinary 2026 season, where he further set records with his remarkable prize money earnings.
stories.bodyText:
Alexander Zverev finally got his hands on the US Open trophy that once seemed destined to be his, overcoming American hope and his own painful Grand Slam history to beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 in Sunday’s final at Flushing Meadows.
Six years after blowing a two-set lead against Dominic Thiem in the 2020 US Open final, Zverev completed one of the biggest pieces of unfinished business in his career. The German, who became a Grand Slam champion at Roland Garros earlier this year, added a second major title in New York to cap a remarkable 2026 season.
“I think God has seen how hard we worked, how much we suffered, how much pain we went through and I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before,” Zverev said during the trophy presentation.
The victory also ended an extraordinary run of disappointment in Grand Slam finals for Zverev, who had previously reached the championship match at the US Open in 2020 and the French Open in 2024 before finally breaking through in Paris this year.
Zverev silences partisan New York crowd
The home crowd had been desperate to see Shelton end a 23-year wait for an American man’s Grand Slam title. The eighth seed was attempting to become the first American man to win a major since Andy Roddick at the 2003 US Open and the first Black American man to win the title since Arthur Ashe in 1968.
But Zverev refused to be intimidated by the partisan atmosphere.
“I know that today 99.9% of the people wanted Ben to win so I'm very sorry,” Zverev said. “Even though I know that the crowd was against me, the crowd was always incredibly fair and we as players we appreciate it.”
The German made the perfect start, capitalising on Shelton’s nerves in his first Grand Slam final. Shelton double-faulted on break point in the opening game and Zverev held his advantage throughout the set, closing it out when the American committed another double fault.
Zverev’s composure became even more evident in the second set. With the crowd attempting to lift Shelton and occasionally reacting loudly to Zverev’s mistakes, the top seed remained focused and raced through the tiebreak, taking a 5-0 lead before closing it 7-2.
Ben Shelton (AP Photo)
Shelton fights back but Zverev refuses to crack
Shelton, however, refused to surrender.
Zverev looked on course for a straight-sets victory after saving a break point with a stunning backhand winner in the sixth game of the third set. Shelton then slipped and crashed to the court, but the setback appeared to galvanise him.
The American began finding greater depth and power from the baseline, eventually breaking Zverev for the first and only time in the match. He held his nerve to take the third set 7-5 and send the final into a fourth.
But the comeback ended there.
Zverev immediately broke Shelton’s serve at the start of the fourth set and then survived a 25-shot rally to strengthen his grip on the match. The German never relinquished the advantage, eventually closing out the contest 6-2.
In an almost surreal moment, Zverev initially did not realise he had won. After Shelton sent a return long on match point, Zverev instinctively moved back towards the baseline as if preparing to receive another serve.
Only after the umpire announced, “Game, set and match Zverev”, and the crowd rose to applaud, did the German realise the title was his. He smiled, raised his arms and headed to the net to embrace Shelton.
From 2020 heartbreak to 2026 glory
The triumph erased one of the most painful chapters of Zverev’s career. In 2020, he led Thiem by two sets and came within two points of victory before becoming the first man since 1949 to lose a Grand Slam final after taking the opening two sets.
This time, there was no collapse.
Zverev has now gone 25-2 in Grand Slam matches in 2026, having won the French Open, reached the Wimbledon final and followed that run by claiming his second major title in New York.
He also collected a record $5.5 million winner’s prize, matching women’s champion Elena Rybakina’s payout from Saturday as the biggest prize in Grand Slam history.
Shelton, meanwhile, leaves New York with a breakthrough of his own despite falling short. He had stunned defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set quarter-final that ended at 3:33 a.m., but could not complete the ultimate upset.
“You’re one of the very best players in the world, maybe the best player in the world this year,” Shelton told Zverev.
For Zverev, there was no better way to answer the ghosts of 2020 than by finally lifting the US Open trophy.
“We went 30 years without winning a Slam title and now won two in the span of three months,” he said.

stories.headline: Swedish election ends in near dead heat; preliminary results give opposition 1-seat majority
stories.deck: The outcome of the election may not be decided until Wednesday (September 16), when local election boards count early votes that did not make it to the polling stations by Election Day. This includes, among others things, overseas votes
stories.bodyText:
Sweden's national election was too close to call early on Monday (September 14, 2026), with preliminary results giving the left-wing opposition a razor-thin one-seat advantage over Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right wing coalition and days of uncertainty until the final ballots are counted.
Preliminary results showed a very narrow lead for the opposition and former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson's bid to return to office at the head of the left coalition. But Mr. Kristersson also said he would explore "possibilities" given the close result.
With 92% of the vote counted early on Monday (September 14), the Swedish Election Authority reported the four opposition parties were heading for 175 seats in the 349-seat parliament to 174 seats for the government alliance.
The outcome of the election may not be decided until Wednesday (September 16), when local election boards count early votes that did not make it to the polling stations by Election Day. This includes, among others things, overseas votes.
Ms. Andersson told supporters that "we must wait for the final election result" but added that "right now we are leading ... But we have to wait for the final result." Mr. Kristersson has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party centre-right coalition. It relied on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, an anti-immigration party that has far-right roots but has moved toward the political mainstream, for a parliamentary majority. The Sweden Democrats had been promised Cabinet posts this time if the governing coalition were returned to office.
"When we have the final result it's a good idea to look at possible combinations," he said early on Monday (September 14), adding that "there is a very clear non-socialist majority, or non-left leaning economic majority in the Swedish parliament. And I will actually take note of that and at least figure out whether there are any possibilities." Sweden Democrat's leader Jimmie Åkesson said that "we will not know tonight" who will form the next government. The party's support slipped almost 3% from its 2022 result of 20.5% and it fell from second to third place.
Exit polls from public broadcaster SVT had initially shown the left-wing parties ahead by several percentage points. The exit polls set off jubilation at the Social Democrats' election gathering but the mood shifted to quiet waiting as the results indicated a closer race.
The centre left Social Democrats have led most Swedish governments since World War II. Ms. Andersson served as Prime Minister from 2021 until she lost power at the last election. To return to office she would have to seal a coalition agreement with other parties.
There are two major political blocs: one with four parties on the right and another with four parties on the left. So the big question is less about which party wins and more about which side can form a majority. Individual parties need a minimum of 4% of the vote to win parliamentary seats.
With broad political consensus in Sweden on several major issues such as support for Ukraine and the country's decision to join NATO, much election discussion focused on the possibility of the anti-immigration hard right entering government. The Sweden Democrats' role was in focus against a background of gains for the populist right in Europe, including the first-place finish by the far-right Alternative for Germany party in a regional election there on September 6.
The Sweden Democrats were founded in the 1980s by people who had been active in right-wing extremist groups, including neo-Nazis. They toned down their rhetoric and expelled openly racist members under Mr. Åkesson, who has led them since 2005 and overseen their growth from what was once a marginal party.
More than 8 million people in the nation of about 10.6 million were eligible to vote.
Published - September 14, 2026 06:41 am IST

briefs.headline: Indonesia rescuers searching for 129 people still missing after passenger ship capsizes
briefs.bodyText: Jakarta: More than 600 Indonesian rescuers were searching for 129 people still missing after a passenger ship capsized in the Java Sea on the weekend, an official said on Monday, with the death toll steady at six.The Virgo Transport 8 ship carrying 243 people went missing in bad weather early on Sunday, the rescue agency said. Authorities have rescued 108 people from the ship, which was travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan..Indonesia passenger ship carrying 243 goes missing in Java Sea amid bad weather."We have continued the search for the missing since early in the morning. We are deploying 622 personnel and around 12 ships," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin rescue agency, told Reuters.He said there was no increase in the death toll of six as of Monday morning.In a video shared by the rescue agency, a large red-and-black ship lies capsized and partially submerged in choppy blue water, with its red-painted underside visible above the surface.Two small boats, each carrying people, were seen floating near the capsized ship amid rough water.On Sunday, Edy Prakoso, another official at the national rescue agency, said the ship leaned heavily to one side after strong waves hit its starboard side.A passing helicopter reported the vessel had capsized, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said on Sunday, with the cause still being investigated.Indonesia relies on ferries across its 17,000 islands, where sea travel is cheaper and more accessible than flying, and there have been numerous accidents.In separate incidents last month, two ferries carrying hundreds of passengers caught fire in waters. Five people died when a ferry caught fire off Madura island, while one person died in a fire on a ferry travelling from the tourist island of Bali.

briefs.headline: ‘We can’t receive it from him’: Why India snubbed Mohsin Naqvi again
briefs.deck: India's women's cricket team made headlines by declining to participate in the Women's Asia Cup trophy presentation, standing in unity with the men's team from last year. The BCCI secretary linked this move to current military tensions with a neighboring nation. Celebrating their impressive eighth Women's Asia Cup title, the team now looks ahead to the Asian Games, with a focus on capturing gold.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
India’s women’s cricket team’s decision not to receive the Women’s Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council president Mohsin Naqvi
 was a show of solidarity with the men’s team, which took the same position after winning the Asia Cup last year, 
BCCI
 secretary Devajit Saikia said.
“Our men’s team won the Asia Cup a year and a half ago. And our whole situation, since the April 2025 Pahalgam incident, changed after that. So, after that, there was pressure on us from our citizens that we shouldn’t keep any relations with our neighboring country and not play cricket with them. But our government has a policy that we must play against every country in multinational tournaments...” Saikia told IANS hours after India beat Sri Lanka in Sunday's final.
“But that doesn’t mean we will follow every condition laid out for us. Our military conflict is still ongoing. One of the main leaders who is working against the interests of our country; we can’t receive the trophy from him. The Women’s team has expressed solidarity with the decision taken by the men’s team last year,” Saikia said.
The decision brought back memories of the controversial presentation after the men's Asia Cup final in 2025. India had beaten Pakistan in the final, but the players were left waiting for more than an hour to receive the trophy and medals.
This time, India had completed a comfortable 72-run victory over Sri Lanka to win a record-extending eighth Women's Asia Cup title. Harmanpreet Kaur and her teammates celebrated on the field, but the Indian side did not collect the trophy from Naqvi during the presentation.
Naqvi was present at the stadium as India sealed the title and was seated alongside dignitaries including BCCI vice-president Rajeev Shukla and Saikia. He later went on stage and handed the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu. The presentation then ended without India receiving the trophy from him.
Saikia said the decision did not take away from the team's performance.
“It doesn’t diminish the performances of our team. We have won all our matches in a one-sided manner. Women’s cricket has been growing so well in India and there’s no bigger evidence of that than this. Our whole planning is geared towards the 2026 ICC T20 World Cup. The happiest part of this tournament is how India has left everyone else behind and surged so far ahead.”
The presence of Naqvi alongside Saikia and Shukla in the Royal Box during the match also led to questions about the interaction between the officials.
“It’s not as if we wouldn’t meet anyone. I was sitting outside in the Royal Box seats right from the toss until the end of the game. Having sat there, I remained in that same place throughout the match. Everyone who came met me during the match; someone sat next to me, then Shukla came and sat with me. The person you mentioned also came and sat alongside Deputy Chairman Khalid (Khalid Al Zarooni) sahib. That’s just a normal tradition—whenever anyone comes, we meet and talk with everyone,” Saikia said.
Saikia said there had been an attempt to resolve the trophy presentation issue.
“We tried to solve today's situation, but our efforts were not successful. We don’t have any regrets. Our ultimate priority and ambition was not to focus on who would give the trophy. We wanted the Indian team to win and we’ve achieved that.”
He also said his interaction with Naqvi was not centred on the trophy. Saikia had presented the fielding medal after the game and said the conversation around that was about India's next assignment.
“I also got the chance to give the fielding medal that’s given out after every game. The conversation that was had around that was about the Asian Games, not about whether the trophy should be taken or not.”
India's attention now shifts to the Asian Games in Japan's Aichi Prefecture. The team is scheduled to play on September 18, 20 and 22.
“Currently, there are no such plans. Right now, our focus is on tomorrow, as our team will be leaving for Japan via Delhi. So, all our attention is set on the Asian Games starting in Japan, where our matches are scheduled for the 18th, 20th and 22nd. Our goal is to bring home the gold medal, and that is our sole objective.”

briefs.headline: Jharkhand LoP accuses Soren-led govt. of protecting influential people amid CID probe into job exam ‘irregularities’
briefs.deck: Babulal Marandi He also urged the Chief Minister not to force students and the unemployed to take to the streets again; called for an immediate recommendation for a CBI inquiry
briefs.bodyText:
Leader of the Opposition in Jharkhand Assembly Babulal Marandi on Sunday (September 13, 2026) alleged a cover-up and protection of influential people in the ongoing Crime Investigation Department (CID) probe into the alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) recruitment exams.
Mr. Marandi also questioned the lack of videography during the statement-recording process. He added that the direction of the probe suggests an exercise aimed solely at suppressing the truth and shielding “big fish.”
In a post on X, Mr. Marandi said that complaints are surfacing which confirm earlier apprehensions. He noted that when individuals detained or interrogated in the case reveal details regarding bribery transactions and the involvement of high-profile politicians, officials, or their intermediaries, those specific parts are being omitted from their recorded statements.
He mentioned that some junior officials involved in the investigation have —on the condition of anonymity— reported that their senior departmental officers are pressuring them not to include such statements in the official record.
“If these complaints are true, it constitutes a grave matter of suppressing the truth and protecting influential people under the guise of an investigation, “ he wrote.
Mr. Marandi asserted that the process of recording statements in such a sensitive case should be videographed and the original recordings must be preserved without any tampering, trimming, or editing to ensure that no official can alter—or cause to be altered—anyone’s statement for their own convenience.
“However, according to the complaints received, this is not happening. Why is there such anxiety to exclude a prominent name from the record the moment it is mentioned? Is the investigation being conducted to reveal the truth or to shield certain individuals?”Mr. Marandi asked.
He further added that serious allegations had previously arisen regarding the role of former Jharkhand DGP Anurag Gupta.
“He is involved in scandalous misdeeds—specifically concerning steering the investigation in the wrong direction, destroying evidence, and denying the existence of the recruitment scam. The shift in the CID’s stance following the protest by the students and the unemployed has further deepened these questions,”Mr. Marandi said.
The former Chief Minister also said, “Now, regarding the CID investigation led by another tainted officer, Manoj Kaushik, complaints are emerging that ‘small fish’ are being made scapegoats to shield the ‘big fish’. These grievances must be addressed through impartial action and the preservation of evidence. Merely showcasing the arrests of low-level individuals will not dispel the apprehension.”
Senior IPS officer of ADG rank Mr. Kaushik is leading the seven-member team probing alleged irregularities in the JPSS and JSSC recruitment examinations.
Giving a warning to the investigating officer, Mr. Marandi said if there is any ongoing game of dropping names from statements, erasing digital evidence, or pressuring individuals to give fabricated statements, it must stop immediately.
He added that there is also a word of advice for the next generation of officers: “do not stake your service, reputation, and conscience merely to curry favour with those in power.”
He also urged Chief Minister Hemant Soren not to force students and the unemployed to take to the streets again. He called for an immediate recommendation for a CBI inquiry and insisted on ensuring arrangements to secure and preserve all original statements, video recordings, and digital evidence.

Mumbai on ‘orange’ alert as IMD warns of heavy rain in parts of Maharashtra
briefs.deck: Moderate rain likely on Sept. 14; rainfall intensity is expected to ease thereafter across the State
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai remained on an orange alert on Sunday (September 13, 2026) with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places, even as several other districts in Maharashtra faced warnings for heavy rain, thunderstorms and lightning until 8.30 a.m. on Monday (September 14, 2026).
The Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC), Mumbai, in its evening district forecast issued at 6 p.m., said heavy to very heavy rain was “very likely” at isolated places in Mumbai. Rainfall intensity is expected to ease thereafter, with moderate rain forecast for September 14, light to moderate rain on September 15 and 16, and light rain on September 17.
The IMD’s official district-warning portal also listed September 13 among the current warning dates.
The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), meanwhile, said a 4.46-metre-high tide occurred at 1.05 p.m. on Sunday, followed by a low tide of 0.44 metres at 7.13 p.m. The next high tide was expected at 1.38 a.m. on Monday (September 14, 2026), it said, when the sea level is forecast to reach 4.43 metres, followed by a 1.21-metre low tide at 7.17 a.m.
The IMD has warned that spells of heavy rain can lead to localised waterlogging or flooding in low-lying and urban areas, traffic and transport disruptions, the uprooting of weak trees and damage to poorly maintained structures. It also cautioned about rough sea conditions along the Konkan coast and the possibility of landslides or rockfalls in vulnerable areas.
In the Mumbai Metropolitan Region and adjoining Konkan belt, Thane is was forecast to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places, while Raigad could see isolated heavy rain.
Palghar faced a more severe forecast, with thunderstorms and lightning accompanied by heavy to extremely heavy rainfall at one or two places.
Elsewhere in Maharashtra, Nandurbar was placed in the highest warning category shown in the IMD bulletin, with thunderstorms, lightning and heavy to extremely heavy rain forecast at one or two places. The Nashik ghats could face heavy to extremely heavy rain along with thunderstorms and lightning, while Dhule could receive heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and gusty winds of 40-50 kmph.
Heavy rain accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of up to 40-50 kmph was also forecast at isolated places in Jalgaon, Nashik, the Pune ghats, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Jalna. Similar heavy-rain and thunderstorm warnings were in place in parts of Vidarbha, including Akola, Amravati, Buldhana and Washim.
The overall intensity is expected to reduce considerably from Monday (September 14, 2026) in most parts of the State.

stories.headline: Firm’s cosmetic promise falls flat, Bengaluru woman wins Rs 1.8 lakh
stories.deck: A woman was led to believe that a cosmetic procedure would yield guaranteed results; however, the clinic failed to provide the expected improvements. After she paid extra for a second treatment that was never carried out, she sought justice from a consumer forum. The ruling was clear: the clinic must refund her full payment and provide compensation for their failure to deliver.
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A visit to treat pigmentation turned into a costly ordeal for a Kadugodi resident after a clinic allegedly upsold her on an expensive cosmetic procedure, assuring her of guaranteed results that never materialised.
The IV additional district consumer disputes redressal commission has ordered a refund, holding that a firm promise of guaranteed results cannot be withdrawn after a consumer has paid for the procedure.
It all began in March 2025, when Sultana (name changed), a Kadugodi resident, approached the clinic for treatment of facial pigmentation. A representative recommended a package comprising ENNO Peeling and PRP (platelet-rich plasma) sessions.
During the consultation, clinic staff also recommended CoolSculpting, a non-invasive fat-reduction treatment.
Assured that the procedure would deliver effective results, Sultana underwent CoolSculpting on her upper abdomen at a cost of Rs 82,000. The treatment was financed through VLCC’s partner FIBE under an agreement signed on March 14.
When the treatment began on April 5, the technician handling her session allegedly told Sultana that treating only the upper abdomen would leave the results looking incomplete and uneven. 
She was therefore advised to undergo the procedure on her lower abdomen as well.
Acting on this advice, Sultana paid an additional Rs 82,000, taking her total payment to Rs 1.6 lakh.
The second payment was also financed through the same loan facility. She was assured that visible results would emerge within 90 days, by the end of May 2025.
However, even after the promised period had elapsed, Sultana saw no improvement. When she raised the issue with the clinic, VLCC allegedly acknowledged it and assured her of a repeat session. That session, however, was never provided.
Adding to her troubles, Sultana discovered that a “loan processing fee” of Rs 12,240 had also been charged to her. When she withheld an EMI payment in July 2025 in protest, she allegedly faced pressure and threats of legal action.
Her efforts to resolve the dispute through emails, personal visits and two complaints to National Consumer Helpline went largely unanswered.
A legal notice issued by her on Nov 1 was also returned unserved. Sultana then filed a consumer complaint on Dec 17, 2025, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
In its defence, VLCC contended that the treatments had been performed in accordance with accepted cosmetology practices.
It argued that Sultana had voluntarily opted for the procedures and signed consent forms acknowledging that results could vary. The company also contended that she had produced no expert opinion establishing negligence.
The consumer forum observed that VLCC had not denied promising results within 90 days.
“Cosmetic procedures carry inherent biological variances, but the OP (opposite party) cannot commercially exploit a consumer by promising specific timelines only to back out later,” it noted.
The commission also found that after the first procedure failed, the clinic marketed a second, costlier treatment instead of offering a remedy or refund.
The bench, comprising president Ramachandra MS and members Nandini H Kumbhar and Savitha Airani, directed VLCC Ltd to refund Rs 1.7 lakh.
It also awarded Rs 10,000 for deficiency in service, Rs 3,000 for mental agony and hardship, and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.

stories.headline: For 18 yrs, a Muslim woman has led Ganeshotsav in Karnataka's Chikkamagaluru
stories.deck: Jubeeda, the panchayat president of Narasimharajapura's Muslim town, spearheads the Ganesh Chaturthi festivities, a role she has proudly held for the last eighteen years. The annual collaboration between Hindu and Muslim community members to install the Ganesha idol exemplifies a remarkable bond of unity. This celebration strengthens interfaith respect and highlights their shared values.
stories.bodyText:
CHIKKAMAGALURU: This 
Ganesh Chaturthi
, a small town in coffee district of Chikkamagaluru is making waves of amity and harmony. Narasimharajapura town panchayat president Jubeeda, a Muslim, has been leading Ganeshotsav celebrations for 18 years as committee president, and she is all geared up for the festival on Monday.
Under the banner of Rajeeva Nagar Sri Vinayaka Seva Samiti, Jubeeda brings together both Hindu and Muslim communities to install the Ganesha idol at a pandal every year.
The committee conducts three days of puja, wraps it with a Satyanarayana puja before immersing the idol as has been the tradition for many years.
"I'm an Indian first. Religion and caste count much later. Along with my religion, I equally respect other religions. For me, humanity is above caste and religion. If we go for Hindu festivals in the town, they come and make Muslim festivals grand. All communities are living in harmony," Jubeeda, 52, said.
Jubeeda's secular spirit is not limited to Ganeshotsav. She works as office-bearer for Kartik Deepotsava (which is conducted around Deepavali) at Nagara Banashankari temple in the same locality of the town.
Her syncretic outlook has won praise from across the spectrum. 
"Jubeeda shares a cordial bond with people of all faiths and takes part in their joys and sorrows.
She actively participates in pujas and decorates her house with lamps during Deepavali. Those who sow seeds of poison between religions should learn from her," said HL Deepak, president, Vidya Ganesh Seva Samiti, Kudregundi, a village in the district.

stories.headline: 529 child labourers rescued in Bengaluru; 105 cases registered
stories.bodyText:
As many as 529 child labourers were rescued and 105 cases registered against employers during a special operation conducted by the Bengaluru City Police on Saturday.
The operation was carried out on September 12 on the directions of senior police officers. Special teams comprising police personnel and Labour Department officials conducted surprise inspections at 6,076 commercial establishments, industrial areas and other locations across the city.
The rescued children were found working at different establishments, following which they were taken into the care of the authorities concerned for further action.
The police said 105 cases have so far been registered against shop owners and other employers who allegedly engaged children as labourers. The cases have been booked under provisions of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act and the Juvenile Justice Act.
Among the city divisions, the West Division recorded the highest number of rescued children at 103, followed by north with 66, central with 63, south with 52 and north-east with 47.
The CCB rescued 45 children and registered the highest number of cases at 26, while the East Division rescued 74 children and registered 18 cases. The North-East Division registered 17 cases, while the west registered 15.

stories.headline: 14 lakh groundwater irrigation sources identified in Karnataka
stories.bodyText:
The seventh Minor Irrigation Census and the second Census of Water Bodies in Karnataka have mapped nearly 39,000 lakes and water bodies that come under Minor Irrigation, and 14.18 lakh wells, including borewells and open wells, being used for agricultural activities, across the State.
While the wells mapped to tap underground water systems are for only agricultural activities (urban drinking water borewells not included), the 38,960 water bodies have covered up to 2,000 hectares of command areas. Besides, the Census has identified 77,573 surface water schemes, which include lift irrigation projects.
The data gathered in the Census was funded by the Union Ministry of Jal Shakti and uses 2023-24 as the reference year. The Census covered 30,671 villages, 300 urban local bodies, and 7,128 urban wards. More comparative data and findings of the Census would be available in the coming days, sources said.
“The field work of the Census, completed in August 2026, is aimed at assessing the actual status of the State’s water resources and enabling scientific planning for future irrigation and water conservation initiatives,” said Minor Irrigation and Science and Technology Minister Ajay Singh on Sunday.
“The data must be effectively used to prioritise water security interventions in drought-affected areas, rejuvenation of lakes, groundwater recharge, construction of check dams, and tank filling schemes. We will take steps towards the efficient management of the State’s water resources through data-driven planning and the use of technology,” he said in a press note.
According to the Minister, the data would help with identifying areas where water conservation interventions are most urgently required, where groundwater recharge must be prioritised, and where minor irrigation infrastructure needs to be strengthened.
Earlier in April, the 2025 Groundwater Assessment Report submitted to the government had shown that the overall groundwater extraction had reduced from 68.44% in 2024 to 66.49% in 2025, and the annual groundwater recharge capability had increased from 18.74 billion cubic meters (BCM) in 2024 to 19.28 billion cubic meters, while annual extractable groundwater resources rose from 16.88 BCM to 17.41 BCM.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru’s green brigade: Residents lead plogging in parks and plant herbs
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Citizens once again came together Sunday for a diverse set of activities under 
The Times of India
’s #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks, presented by Multigen, in association with Kristu Jayanti University and supported by Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA).
The morning began with a plog run and waste segregation session at Madhavan Park in Jayanagar and Nagapura Park in Rajajinagar, organised in collaboration with Indian Ploggers Army and Youth For Seva, respectively. Volunteers across age groups collected sacks of plastic waste from the park and highlighted the importance of avoiding single-use plastics. The session ended with volunteers pledging to care for their surroundings.
Following the plogging session, the volunteers headed to Kempabudhi Park, which featured plantation activities. The session organised by Adamya Chetana foundation featured an eco-lifestyle talk and planting of medicinal herbs at the park. The team together planted shankupushpa creepers, rosemary, nagadali, lemongrass, nelabasale and vishamooli. The vine plantation was carried out to protect the park’s existing native flora.
Together, the activities reflected the movement’s continued focus on combining environmental action with community participation.
Participants SpeakAkash Mishra, resident of Haralur: This is my first time volunteering with 
TOI
. As we’re already seeing garbage everywhere, I wanted to do something about it. I collected all the waste materials from the park today; it even had glass from car windshields. I wanted to be involved with a group for a long time; this activity was also about educating ourselves. Earlier, even I used to throw away a lot of waste without realising it.
Inchara Swami, engineering student: We covered the entire perimeter of the park today and picked up microplastics. There were many cigarette and gutka packets. It’s my third week here; I’ll continue the activity in future too. We learnt the impact of plastic on the soil and how it is damaging as it doesn’t decompose.
Venkatesh Prasad, resident of SR Nagar: A huge number of our people don’t have proper civic sense; the litter here has come from all age groups. Children throw chocolate wrappers and adults throw alcohol bottles and gutka packets... I want the next generation to have better civic sense, I’m here for Gen Z.
Lalriatpui Molsom, resident of Jayanagar: I always like social activities; this is the second time I’ve joined the 
TOI
 initiative. Clean parks are very important for a peaceful mind. If you cannot achieve cleanliness through advice and awareness, we can at least show others and help them understand the value of clean parks. Seeing a clean park, I feel refreshed.
Dilip Kumar Mishra, resident of BTM Layout: Our environment is getting totally destroyed by population and vehicles, so definitely we have to come out of our homes; otherwise, our future will be affected. The biggest message of today’s activity is that people should take care of spaces near their homes and take responsibility. Instead of going somewhere else in the morning, we should do something for the betterment of environment and for clean oxygen near our homes.
Kumaraswamy S, Adamya Chetana member: The initiative is effective; today, we planted around 10 kinds of plants around the park. The message is that as nature and human beings coexist, we should not destroy nature and should instead be part of it and restore it. We need to plant as many trees as possible because every human needs at least 700kg of oxygen every year. A healthy tree can give 100kg of oxygen in a year; for each person, there should be seven trees; but it is not the case now.

briefs.headline: Audio advertisements coming soon to Bengaluru’s BMTC buses
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Those using buses for their everyday commute could soon be forced to listen to audio advertisements during their journey. Last week, Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) floated a tender seeking an agency to run an in-bus audio advertisement system across its fleet.
In its initial phase, ads will be played in 300 non-AC BMTC buses across Bengaluru. The selected bidder will supply, install, operate and maintain the entire system — the first of its kind in South India. BMTC in the tender document stated that the primary objective of advertising is to generate non-fare revenue.
These advertisements will be spread across BMTC’s ordinary, express and night service buses, with each audio slot in Kannada lasting up to 10 seconds per minute. English translation can be optional. The fee will be charged per bus per month. The selected licensee will get a three-year contract, which could be extended further. Through this system, BMTC also plans to enable targeted location-based advertising by integrating it with existing GPS systems. Ads will be played in such a way that passenger announcements remain seamless without any interference.
About 10% of the advertising airtime will be reserved by BMTC for its own announcements, public service messages and authorised communications. 
The utility also plans to expand the service to more buses in future.
While BMTC assures that it will maintain passenger comfort through regulated volume, content quality and language compliance, commuters feel concerned it might impact their journeys. “During peak-hour travel, if these ads are noisy and start disturbing passengers, I feel this could lead to friction between them and the conductor. It should also not cause any hindrance to the stop announcements,” Rahul S, from the commuter group Friends of BMTC, said.
Akshay Bharadwaj K, a regular commuter from Magadi Road, said these ads could take a toll on passengers. “BMTC commuters already deal with a lot of noise, including honking, traffic sounds and chattering inside the bus. Playing ads will worsen the problem. I don’t want this to happen,” he added.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru’s rejuvenated Ulsoor lake readies for immersion of 1 lakh Ganesha idols
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: Months after rejuvenation efforts at Ulsoor lake, civic authorities are preparing to receive over one lakh Ganesha idols during this year’s Gowri-Ganesha festival, while attempting to ensure the waterbody does not bear the environmental cost of the celebrations.
Bengaluru Central City Corporation (BCCC) has announced that idol immersion at the specially constructed kalyani within the lake premises will be permitted on select days.
Officials said the dedicated kalyani, measuring about 5.5 metres in depth and spread across nearly 650sqft, has been prepared to handle the large inflow of idols expected over the 15-day festival period. Authorities estimate that more than one lakh idols could reach the immersion point this year.
“Extra precautions have been taken to ensure the lake does not get polluted and all Ganesh idols are immersed only in the kalyani. We have arranged mobile tanks at four sides of the lake so that smaller idols can be immersed there itself,” said a lake engineer with BCCC.
The corporation has reiterated that only eco-friendly idols will be permitted for immersion. Officials warned that PoP idols found on sale would be seized and legal action initiated against violators.
Immersion is allowed only on alternate days
Authorities have scheduled Ganesha idol immersion at Ulsoor Lake kalyani only on Sept 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 27 and 28. Immersion will not be permitted on other days for cleaning of the kalyani, removal of idol remnants and festival waste, and maintenance of the rejuvenated lake surroundings.
Arrangements for crowd management
- Two cranes have been deployed for round-the-clock operations at the immersion site
- A separate queue system has been created for smaller idols
- Footpaths around the lake have been barricaded and access routes regulated to streamline movement of devotees
- Mobile tankers have been stationed around the lake
- Solid waste management teams and autos will be deployed to collect festival waste
- The corporation has installed CCTV cameras, arranged ambulance services, improved lighting around the lake premises, and made provisions for drinking water and mobile toilets
- Traffic and law-and-order arrangements are being coordinated with police and other departments
- A single-window committee comprising officials from the corporation, police, Bescom, fire and emergency services and other agencies has been formed to grant permissions for Ganesha installations and oversee festival-related arrangements

briefs.headline: Six years without civic council: Who speaks for Bengaluru’s wards?
briefs.deck: The absence of elected representatives has left gaps in neighbourhood-level grievance redressal, civic oversight, local planning and accountability
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru has gone six years without an elected civic council, after the term of the erstwhile Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) council ended on Sept 10, 2020. The administrative machinery has continued to run the city, but a key layer of local governance has been missing: elected representatives whose mandate is to speak for individual wards.
Councillors were the first political point of contact for residents, following up on complaints, identifying local needs, monitoring works, and pushing for funds. Their absence has increasingly drawn MLAs into neighbourhood-level issues, even though legislators have a wider mandate and primary responsibility for lawmaking.
The gap extends beyond individual complaints. It raises questions about who supervises civic officials at the ward level, how local priorities are translated into projects, how civic money is monitored, and whether residents have a meaningful role in deciding what gets done in their neighbourhoods.
With chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 saying elections to the city’s five corporations will not be delayed further, attention is now turning to when Bengaluru will regain an elected local govt. There is also uncertainty over whether the ward-level political map could change following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Missing Third Tier
Local govt is the tier closest to citizens. Its significance lies in being able to deal with problems that are too localised for state-level political representatives but too important to leave entirely to officials. 
Former mayor Gangambike Mallikarjun questioned why local elections could remain pending for years when elections to Parliament and state legislatures are held on schedule.
Former Hoodi corporator AC Hariprasad pointed to the original logic of decentralisation: local representatives are physically closer to residents and can respond to everyday concerns such as water supply and garbage.
The absence of this political layer also means residents have fewer avenues for participating in decisions about their own neighbourhoods.
No One To Approach
For a resident dealing with a blocked drain, overflowing garbage, a damaged road or a missing streetlight, the difference is practical: there is no councillor responsible for taking up the issue.
A councillor’s role was not limited to receiving complaints. Regular visits to different parts of a ward allowed problems to be identified before they became complaints, while follow-up with officials helped push them towards resolution.
The deterioration of solid waste management illustrates the problem. The lack of a regular political presence, Gangambike Mallikarjun said, has made it harder to monitor garbage collection across neighbourhoods.
Padmanabhanagar resident Lalitha Rao said the disconnect is also visible in the choice of civic works. Projects proposed by the govt may proceed, she said, but there is no equivalent mechanism for identifying and pushing for what a particular neighbourhood needs.
110 Villages, Bigger Needs
The problem becomes more pronounced in the 110 villages that were brought into the erstwhile BBMP in 2008.
Many of these areas entered the civic system with substantial deficits in basic infrastructure. Roads and water supply remain among the concerns, while the scale of the requirement often calls for sustained intervention rather than individual fixes.
Hariprasad said this was precisely where ward-level representation mattered most. Councillors could identify gaps, make a case for projects and seek funds for neighbourhood infrastructure, including parks and lakes.
Who’s Watching Officials?
The missing councillor is also a missing layer of oversight. According to Hariprasad, ward engineers, health inspectors and solid waste management supervisors earlier came under the direct supervision of elected representatives. That relationship gave residents someone who could be held responsible for following up when officials failed to respond.
There was another, less formal incentive: competition between councillors. Hariprasad said representatives competed to secure funds and complete works in their wards, and this pressure could translate into better outcomes.
The question extends to money as well. Former Malleswaram corporator Manjunath Raju said the absence of elected representatives has made it less clear who is monitoring civic budgets and what criteria are being used to decide which works receive priority.
Local Govt’s Wider Role
The ward-level representative is also part of a broader system of local social and economic planning. Civic Bangalore founder Kathyayani Chamaraj said the local govt has a role in identifying people who need ration cards, pensions and other welfare measures, apart from planning for economic development and social justice.
She also pointed to the loss of area sabhas under the GBA Act, which had provided a mechanism for residents to participate in planning and monitoring works. The issue, therefore, is not simply whether a road gets repaired or garbage gets cleared. It is whether residents have an elected institution through which their priorities, welfare needs and local concerns can enter the decision-making process.
Question B’luru Is Left With
Bengaluru’s civic administration has not stopped functioning. What has disappeared is the elected intermediary between that administration and the people it serves.
That distinction is at the heart of the debate over the long-delayed polls: who identifies what a ward needs, who presses officials to deliver it, who scrutinises the spending and, ultimately, who answers to the people living there?
Bengaluru’s civic elections: A history of interrupted terms
An analysis of Bengaluru’s civic election history since 1970 shows a recurring pattern: polls have rarely followed a predictable cycle, with successive state govts allowing elected terms to lapse, and changes to the city’s boundaries and governance structure repeatedly resetting the electoral process.
■ 1970 | Civic polls held: Elections to the then Bangalore City Corporation (BCC) were held. Successive state govts did not conduct subsequent polls on time
■ 1983 | Polls return: BCC elections were held within months of Ramakrishna Hegde becoming CM
■ 1989 | Corporation expanded: BCC was expanded and became Bangalore Mahanagara Palike (BMP)
■ 1990 | First expanded BMP election: Elections to the expanded BMP held
■ Oct 1996 | Another election: BMP elections were held, but the next regular cycle would again be disrupted
■ 2007-08 | BBMP takes shape: Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) was formed by bringing together BMP, seven CMCs, a TMC and 110 villages
■ 2010 | First BBMP election: First election to the newly formed BBMP was held for 198 wards
■ 2015 | Second BBMP election: The second and last BBMP election was held for 198 wards
■ Sept 10, 2020 | Elected council ends: The term of elected BBMP council expired. No subsequent civic election held
■ 2022 | 243-ward plan: The 198-ward BBMP was restructured as govt took up delimitation for 243 wards
■ 2023 | Another reset: Govt scrapped the 243-ward plan and undertook fresh delimitation for 225 wards
■ 2025 | Greater Bengaluru framework: Greater Bengaluru Governance Act came into effect, paving the way for Greater Bengaluru Authority and five city corporations with 369 wards
■ 2026 | Still no elected council: Bengaluru remains without an elected civic council. Elections are now due for the five corporations under the GBA framework
Stakeholders Speak
‘
Maneyolage maneyodeya iddano illavo
…’ This vachana by Basavanna, which metaphorically talks about how a house accumulates waste in the absence of its owner, sums up the situation in today’s wards. Even as the Bengaluru development minister has taken up initiatives, the essential local-level coordination could have been achieved by corporators: 
Gangambike Mallikarjun, former mayor.
Ward engineers, health inspectors and solid waste management supervisors were under the direct control of the corporator. In the absence of corporators, we often see poor response from officials when the public approaches them. There was also a healthy competition among corporators to obtain funds and get works done in their wards. That competition benefited the city: 
AC Hariprasad, former corporator, Hoodi.
Citizens don’t know whom to approach with their issues. MLAs cannot take care of everything as they are primarily meant for legislation, and they aren’t always approachable. With no elected corporators, there is also no clarity on who is monitoring budgets and what parameters are being considered for implementation: 
Manjunath Raju, former corporator, Malleswaram.
The GBA Act has done away with area sabhas, where every voter could participate in planning and monitoring of works. The third tier of govt is not just about civic issues, but also about planning for economic development and social justice as a local self-govt:
 Kathyayani Chamaraj, founder, Civic Bangalore.
There’s nobody to approach with our complaints. Generally, what govt proposes as work is being done, but nobody is looking at the local requirements and proposing projects or interventions accordingly: 
Lalitha Rao, resident of Padmanabhanagar.

briefs.headline: 800 child labourers, 503 from Bengaluru alone, rescued in two-hour crackdown across Karnataka
briefs.deck: In a Statewide crackdown on child labour on Saturday, police teams and Labour Department officials inspected 16,951 premises across Karnataka and rescued 800 children, all in a matter of two hours, with Bengaluru city alone accounting for 63% of the rescues, at 503
briefs.bodyText:
In a Statewide crackdown on child labour on Saturday, police teams and Labour Department officials inspected 16,951 premises across Karnataka and rescued 800 children, all in a matter of two hours, with Bengaluru city alone accounting for 63% of the rescues, at 503
The crackdown comes against the backdrop of Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar’s surprise visit to the APMC Yard in Yeshwantpur, recently, where officials found 19 children working on the premises. Following this, the Chief Minister had ordered a Statewide crackdown, and the action on Saturday covered markets, eateries, workshops, construction sites, garages, welding shops and small industrial establishments.
The special drive was conducted between 10 a.m. and noon across 962 police stations.
Bengaluru marks highest
Bengaluru city recorded the highest number, with 503 children rescued. The police teams inspected 5,897 premises across 188 police station limits.
A total of 18 cases were registered under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 and the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015.
The rescued children belonged to Karnataka, Bihar, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Assam, Jharkhand, and Nepal. “A majority of the children rescued are from hotels, restaurants, eateries, petrol pumps, grocery stores and warehouses. They had been employed because they can be paid far less than adults,” said Bengaluru Police Commissioner Seemanth Kumar Singh.
“The rescue operation was categorised under hazardous and non-hazardous occupations. In cases involving hazardous employment, FIRs have been registered against the employers. Employers found engaging children in non-hazardous work have been issued notices,” another senior officer, who was part of the operation, told The Hindu.
Vijayapura, Tumakuru
Vijayapura district reported the second-most number of rescues, with 72, after inspections at 1,156 premises. The district reported 25 instances of action, including three FIRs. Tumakuru district rescued 33 children from 660 premises.
Not a single child labourer was rescued during the drive from KGF, Mysuru, Mandya, Davangere, Hassan, Shivamogga, Uttara Kannada, Chikkamagaluru, Gadag, and Raichur districts
The rescued children have been handed over to the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) for the rehabilitation process.

briefs.headline: Prakash Raj to visit 100 booths in Karnataka to bring evidence of arbitrariness, calls SIR a ‘scam’
briefs.bodyText:
Calling the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) a “scam” and “conspiracy”, actor Prakash Raj said starting September 22 till September 30, he would visit 100 polling booths across Karnataka, and bring evidence on how arbitrarily the exercise has been conducted, which he said he would present as “National public hearing” at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on October 15.
Mr. Raj said he would also take “this fight” legally, after collecting all the evidence at different courts. He pointed out that at these polling booths, he, along with civil society groups, would do “social audit” by mapping the details, looking into each case of how and why the electors were put into the absent, shifted, duplicate, dead or others (ASDDO) list, and look into the enumeration forms of those who got notices to check if they filled them correctly, or even if not, what discrepancy the notice flags. Mr. Raj argued that these mistakes, for which people are queuing up, are not committed by the citizens who are being punished.
VIP treatment
Questioning the VIP treatment to prominent personalities like actor Shiva Rajkumar, the actor questioned if some people are “more equal”. Such people, who are in the Election Commission’s list of VIPs, where officials will come personally and clear the hearing process, should deny this treatment and stand with the public at this time, because this is outright bias against the common citizen.
“Does that mean just because you are popular, you get the privilege? And if you are not popular, if you are a common man, you are underprivileged in this country? Not fair.”
Criticising political parties across the board, he said, “From Rahul Gandhi to Narendra Modi, everyone offers biryani packets when it is about elections, but when it comes to situations where citizens need them, like now, in SIR, during Covid pandemic, they (political parties) leave the public on their own.”
“In a democracy, a voter decides who will govern, but this exercise is aiming to change that. With this, government wants to decide who can vote. Still no opposition party is speaking for their people who elected them,” he argued.
Forced incrimination
Further taking on the design of the exercise, Mr. Raj said the voters who have been deleted and put into the ASDDO list are told to get included through form-6, while the form-6 declaration itself says, “I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the ‘first time‘ and my name is not included in any Assembly constituency/Parliamentary constituency. I am aware that making the above statement or declaration in relation to this application which is false and which I know or believe to be false or do not believe to be true, is punishable under Section 31 of Representation of the People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.”
This way, each voter who is seeking inclusion after being removed is “incriminating“ themselves. Does the Election Commission “technically and legally want each person to lie?” he questioned.
Against claims of inclusion
The actor further pointed to the immunity provided to the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners under Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, which bars courts from entertaining or continuing civil or criminal proceedings against them for acts done or purported to be done in the discharge of their official duties. He said, “Such immunity is planned because they knew they are conspiring a scam, otherwise why else such clause be introduced just months before planning something like this?” he questioned, adding that if it was an inclusionary exercise, the timeline would have supported the claim and not been done in a rush.

stories.headline: Petrol powers half of new cars if hybrids not counted
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Alternative-fuel vehicles may have overtaken petrol cars in India-but only if hybrids are counted as alternatives. FADA's Aug registration data showed petrol's share of passenger-vehicle retail declining to 40.8%, while CNG, electric and hybrid vehicles together reached 41.9%.
The crossover appeared to mark a significant change in India's fuel mix, with alternatives moving ahead of petrol for the first time.
A more granular analysis by JATO Dynamics, however, provides an important counterpoint. Mild and strong hybrids continue to carry petrol engines and require petrol to operate. Once these models are added back to conventional petrol vehicles, petrol-powered cars still account for approximately half the market.
JATO's fuel-wise dataset covered 3,62,763 passenger-vehicle registrations in Aug. Conventional petrol models accounted for 1,49,484 units, or 41.2%. Another 25,070 vehicles, representing 6.9%, were classified as petrol hybrids, while strong hybrids contributed 6,956 units, or 1.9%.
Taken together, these three categories accounted for 1,81,510 registrations - or 50% of the market covered by JATO's fuel-mix data.
"Mild and strong hybrids use electric assistance differently, but both remain fundamentally dependent on an internal-combustion engine and petrol," said Ravi Bhatia, president and CEO of JATO Dynamics India. "They may reduce fuel consumption, but they should not be confused with vehicles that have moved away from petrol." The broader shift remains clear: Conventional petrol-only cars are losing share as CNG, EVs and hybrids expand.

stories.headline: FPIs withdraw 13,100 crore from equities in 2 weeks
stories.bodyText:
New Delhi: Foreign investors pulled out Rs 13,138 crore from Indian equities in the first half of Sept, as heightened global uncertainty pushed crude oil prices higher, while rising US bond yields and a firm dollar weighed on risk appetite.
The latest outflow comes after Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) turned net buyers in July and Aug, infusing Rs 20,200 crore and Rs 29,630 crore, respectively, according to data from the Central Depository Services (India) Ltd (CDSL). Prior to that, FPIs remained net sellers for four consecutive months from March to June.
With the latest withdrawal, the total outflow from Indian equities by FPIs has climbed to Rs 2.4 lakh crore so far in 2026, surpassing the Rs 1.7 lakh crore withdrawn during the entire 2025, the data showed.
Vedant Gupte, co-founder and CEO of investment platform Trackk, said the Sept selling was driven more by global factors than domestic concerns. "Sept selling is a dollar-and-crude story, not an India story. When US yields firm up and oil climbs, money leaves every emerging market," he said.
Brent crude surged to $109.9 per barrel on Friday and continued to remain above $102 per barrel, its July-high level, amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty.
Looking ahead, FPI flows are likely to be influenced by the Iran-US conflict and its impact on crude oil prices. Foreign investors also extended their selling to the debt market.

stories.headline: The evidence gap in dole politics
stories.deck: Governments often attach lofty social purposes such as dignity and empowerment to cash transfers, but rarely publish the model that links payments to outcomes
stories.bodyText:
In May 1795, English magistrates met at the Pelican Inn in Speenhamland, Berkshire. With food prices rising and the French Revolution unsettling the English establishment, they decided to top up agricultural wages from parish funds, linking payouts to bread prices and family size. Hungarian economic historian Karl Polanyi later saw this as an early assertion of a human “right to live” against the harshness of the market.
Critics, however, held a different view. Once wage support, relief for the poor, and public finance were folded into one instrument, it became unclear what the system was protecting: poor families, the wage structure, employers, or social peace. By subsidising wages from public funds, the Speenhamland system blurred price signals and weakened incentives. While relief could be justified, the instrument still had to be judged by its effects. India’s dole politics must now face the same test.
Cash support can indeed be essential in a poor, informal economy. The Economic Survey 2025-26 notes that transfers to women amount to 11-24% of the monthly income of women daily-wage workers, and 11-87% of self-employed women. But a transfer that begins as relief can also become a permanent fiscal commitment unless there is a clear account of who receives it, what it changes, and what it displaces.
These concerns assume importance because dole politics is now a regular feature of Indian statecraft. It appears as free electricity, free bus travel, monthly cash transfers, subsidised food, and utility subsidies.
PRS Legislative Research estimates that unconditional cash transfers to women alone rose from two States in 2022-23 to 12 states in 2025-26, with an estimated annual cost of ₹1.68 lakh crore (about 0.5% of GDP). For example, West Bengal has moved from Lakshmir Bhandar to Annapurna Yojana, budgeting ₹36,000 crore for a ₹3,000 monthly transfer to about 1.3 crore women. Tamil Nadu allocated ₹14,412 crore for the Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thogai in its 2026–27 interim budget, and Assam set aside ₹5,000 crore for Orunodoi. Such schemes stake major claims on State finances.
Need for accountability
Cash may improve welfare, but it should not become a substitute for the public goods that make welfare durable. The same woman who values ₹1,500-₹3,000 may also need a functioning health centre, childcare, a good government school, or access to better work. A cash transfer may soften the strain created by weak institutions, but it cannot, by itself, address them.
Governments often attach lofty social purposes such as dignity and empowerment to these transfers, but rarely publish the model that links payments to outcomes. Who exactly is being targeted? What baseline data justifies the scheme? What effect is anticipated on consumption, debt, nutrition, schooling, health spending, labour supply, or women’s bargaining power? Without such answers, it is unsurprising that much of India’s dole politics today is defended by the moral language of welfare rather than evidence. An ADB study, prepared for the 16th Finance Commission, found that India lacks a systematic dataset of government expenditure on cash-transfer schemes.
Other democracies also redistribute and are not immune to welfare politics. However, benefits such as unemployment insurance, food support, and healthcare subsidies are usually tied to eligibility rules, contribution records, job-search obligations, or periodic reassessment. India need not copy these systems mechanically. Some transfers, especially to women in poor households, may be better left unconditional. But the fewer the conditions placed, the greater must be the obligation on governments to provide evidence.
A large recurring transfer should therefore include a welfare impact statement before rollout, detailing the objective, eligibility rule, expected coverage, five-year fiscal cost, alternatives considered, likely leakage and exclusion errors, and measurable outcomes. After rollout, household surveys should record not only whether the transfer was received but also how it affected consumption, debt, health spending, schooling, mobility, work incentives, control over household expenditure, and subjective well-being. Anonymised microdata should then be made available for independent research. Schemes that spend public money on this scale must survive severe scrutiny.
The case for evidence is also one of democratic fairness. Evidence will not remove politics from welfare, but it could make that politics more honest.
Sayantan Kundu is Assistant Professor of Finance at IMI Kolkata. Amarendu Nandy is Associate Professor of Economics & Public Policy at IIM Ranchi. Views are personal

stories.headline: Tiruppur garment makers, textile mills call for minimum floor price for yarn

Joint Committee of Tiruppur Knitwear and Textile Cluster has urged the Union government to fix a minimum floor price for yarn.
This was one of the decisions taken at a recent meeting of garment manufacturers in Tiruppur and some of the textile mill associations in Tamil Nadu.
With the garment manufacturers saying that they were hit by the frequent and steep hike in cotton yarn prices, the joint committee meeting was organised.
The participants demanded the Union government to permit yarn exports only if the export prices shot up above the minimum floor price, which will take into account the cotton rates.
They also sought removal of import duty on cotton for five years, ensuring Tamil Nadu mills received cotton from the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) on a priority bases, and measures to check sale of cotton purchased by large traders from the CCI for exports and sold at the domestic market for higher prices. The Tamil Nadu government should also procure cotton directly from farmers and supply to the mills in the State, the Committee said.
It asked the textile mills to fix the yarn prices once a month or once every two months rather than revising the rates frequently.
The Union government should form a committee involving all stakeholders to monitor and regulate raw material prices, it added.
